name: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple
tagline: Kerala’s ancient serpent-grove for fertility and bridal blessings
summary: Mannarasala near Haripad is Kerala’s best‑known serpent grove; pilgrims come for fertility, marital blessings and distinctive bridal-life‑cycle offerings and rituals.
description: Mannarasala is an ancient serpent‑shrine and sacred grove near Haripad in Alappuzha district centred on the worship of Lord Sree Nagaraja and associated naga deities. The site is famous for thousands of small snake images, a living tradition of serpent veneration and a unique set of life‑cycle rituals.

Pilgrims come to seek fertility, protection and marital blessings; couples who are childless and brides or families preparing for marriage often perform specific offerings and vows here and return for thanksgiving when prayers are fulfilled. Temple traditions emphasise offerings such as uruli (metal vessel) ceremonies, Noorum Palum (turmeric and milk) and other dedicated vows.

Mannarasala matters as a living cultural site: rituals are rooted in local Illam (ancestral‑house) practices and legend (Parasurama and the Naga‑line), the temple preserves female custodial roles (the Mannarasala Amma/woman priest figure), and festivals such as Ayilyam and Maha Shivaratri remain focal moments for public devotion.

Visitors experience a dense green kavu (grove) threaded with snake images, see ceremonial offerings and processions during festival days, and can observe or participate in prescribed devotional acts (follow temple guidance and local etiquette).
highlights: A living serpent grove with very large numbers of snake images and shrines.
Pilgrimage centre for fertility and marital blessings (offerings and thanksgiving rituals).
Distinctive offerings: uruli kamazhthal, Noorum Palum, puttum‑motta and sarpabali in special cases.
Mannarasala Amma — a prominent female priestly role and custodial family traditions.
Ayilyam festival season (Sept–Oct) and Maha Shivaratri attract the largest crowds.
Strong local lineage (Illam) rituals and vows connecting weddings, childbirth and thanksgiving.

sections.heading: Background
body: Tradition holds that Mannarasala (the ‘cooled earth’ grove) becomes the home of the serpent king after the land of Kerala is made habitable; the temple history and local Illam (ancestral house) practices link Parasurama, a five‑hooded serpent legend and ongoing family custodianship. The site is an enduring centre of naga (serpent) worship in south‑west Kerala.

The temple complex and grove preserve a network of small stone and metal snake images offered by devotees over generations. Mannarasala’s ritual calendar and the role of women from particular families in performing rites are central to how the shrine functions as a living institution.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Walk the shaded kavu and view the countless serpent images, small shrines and the groves where devotees place offerings. Observe or request information about the key rituals: Uruli Kamazhthal (placing/overturning an uruli as a vow for children), Noorum Palum (turmeric and milk offerings), puttum‑motta (small serpent nests with eggs offered by devotees) and, in prescribed circumstances, sarpabali.

During festival days (especially Ayilyam and Maha Shivaratri) you can see processions, special Noorum Palum observances and public rites performed by temple custodians. Many devotees also visit to make vows before marriage or to give thanksgiving offerings after childbirth; these life‑cycle practices are a main reason brides and wedding families visit the shrine.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Mannarasala sits close to Haripad town (Mannarasala P.O., Haripad, Alappuzha). The shrine is active year‑round; the most intense visitation is during the Ayilyam season (roughly Sept–Oct) and on Maha Shivaratri. Expect large crowds during festival days and plan extra time then. Confirm temple opening times, ritual schedules and any visitor rules before you travel.

Follow temple etiquette: remove footwear before entering sacred areas, show respect to ongoing rites and ask permission before photographing inside inner groves or during rituals. Offerings commonly brought by devotees include plantains/bananas and small snake images; the temple website lists formal offerings and vows — confirm permitted items and the procedure at the offerings counter on arrival.

latest.text: Kanni/Ayilyam observances at Mannarasala were listed in the Kerala Tourism 2026‑27 event calendar; Ayilyam remains the principal festival season for large public serpent‑worship rites.
Mannarasala’s festival notices on the temple site list Maha Shivaratri (15 February 2026) as a special day for offerings including the unique Noorum Palum and Sarpabali observances.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Ayilyam season (roughly Sept–Oct) and major festival days; otherwise year‑round (check festival dates).
visitorInfo.howToReach: Mannarasala lies near Haripad in Alappuzha district (Mannarasala P.O.). It is reachable by road from Haripad town (the temple is about 3 km from the Haripad bus area); use local buses, taxis or auto‑rickshaws and confirm local connections on the day of travel.
etiquette: Confirm ritual schedules, opening times and offerings procedure with the temple office before you travel.
Remove footwear and follow the directions of temple staff; ask permission before photographing rituals or inside inner groves.
If you come for fertility or bridal vows, read the temple’s offerings page on uruli, Noorum Palum and the common votive practices so you bring items that comply with temple rules.
During Ayilyam and Shivaratri expect crowds — arrive early and allow time for offering queues and darshan.
